replying_to: Replying to Icy: A benchmark for measuring compositional inductive bias of emergent communication models
display_title: Official Review of Paper337 by Reviewer c4bC

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper seeks to use non compositional perturbations to artificial compositional data in order to measure the compositionality of emergent communication systems. By requiring the communication systems to learn non compositional tasks, we can see that a capacity to represent these data effectively will indicate a lack of compositional inductive bias.
content.main_review:
First, some things I liked about this paper. The results section covers the possibility of model size being the dominating factor in learning these tasks. In 5.4, the authors present evidence that the model architecture is the dominating factor by varying the number of parameters. These experiments were very satisfactory. 5.5 covers inductive bias in the context of limited data resources, and while these experiments would have benefited from a view of sample complexity that covers more than just single data size, I was happy to see it brought in. I would have liked to see some discussion of the models themselves in order to clarify where these inductive biases might come from.

“comp” appears to be a linear translation. I’m unconvinced that this should be considered a compositional grammar at all. Conversely, I felt that the permuted grammar is likely to be compositional if the rules of permutation are consistent (we do consider translation generally to be compositional even though the words are reordered).

The paper seems to heavily abuse the word compositionality, without really describing what it means. Because compositionality itself has many facets, I would like to see a discussion of what particular properties the compositionality metrics are measuring. I would look into https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.08351 both for an in depth discussion of aspects of compositionality and an example of artificial tasks which measure these various aspects. Given that the paper is concerned with artificial tasks in order to measure compositionality, I would consider it highly relevant.

There were a number of references to human perceptions of compositionality (“apparently non compositional to a human”, “neither a human nor compositional metric can recognize …”) but I did not actually see any human trials. 

In terms of presentation: There were several points where I struggled to understand what was happening because of undefined notation. I was uncertain about why you included the work you did in the related work section, while leaving out other crucial related work. I didn’t see this work as being particularly related to probes at all, but I did see it as strongly related to other work that uses artificial data in order to test the capacity and inductive bias of models (as just one example, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.01044.pdf, Examining the Inductive Bias of Neural Language Models with Artificial Languages)

MINOR
- “tabular” should be tabula
- posdis vs PosDis consistency 
- “Section 7” on page three should be in parentheses
- all notation should be introduced in 3.1.1 before being used


QUESTIONS
- What is the “attribute of the utterance” (page 4)?
- What sort of distribution is used as p() in the mutual information computation in 3.2.1?
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper seems incomplete in its analysis and also is not specific in how it defines compositionality. The experiments are reasonably comprehensive but the particular tasks and perturbations selected are not well analyzed in terms of what they tell us about the inductive biases.

**EDIT:** I have raised my score slightly to reflect significant improvement in the paper, through the addition of some human trials and the use of more explicit definitions and reasoning around compositionality. While I don't think that the paper is quite ready, I think that the significant changes show potential value in this work.

replying_to: Replying to Icy: A benchmark for measuring compositional inductive bias of emergent communication models
display_title: Official Review of Paper337 by Reviewer ZwK6

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors begin by making the case that current emergent communication models do not have a proper inductive bias towards compositional languages, but that testing this in general is expensive and difficult, despite the selection of previously proposed metrics for compositonality. They then suggest that by finding a transform that renders a language difficult for humans to learn but just as easy for machines to learn we can measure how "apparently non-compositional" such languages are to humans. In the background section, signaling games and accompanying notation are defined, and related work on compositionality is described, though how exactly the current work fits into the frame given is not made clear.

The authors then describe their methodology, starting with a "perfectly compositional grammar" and listing the transforms they apply to it, including a random baseline, basic permutations of the original,  a random projection transformation of the tokens, cumulative rotation to take advantage of the RNN's accumulated hidden state, and various shuffling transforms. Next, the metrics of composotionality are briefly mentioned and the main neural architectures of interest are described and then examples of the grammars along with the compositionality numbers for these grammars, averaged over 5 random seeds.

The main experiments of the paper revolve around showing that current neural architectures used in emergent communication work can quickly fit languages that the authors consider to be non-composotional. Further experiments are conducted to make sure that the given results are not merely a result of the number of parameters in each model, that fixing the number of training steps does not much change relative performance, and that not updating the hidden state of RNNs shows better compositional inductive bias, according to the metrics in the paper. Additionally, the authors search for models that have low bias against one of the shuffle transforms, with mixed results. Finally, they experiment with supervised training.
content.main_review:
I agree with the authors that a benchmark for measuring the inductive bias towards compositionaly in models used for emergent communication would be quite useful. Furthermore, I agree that current metrics do not properly measure inductive bias implicit in models.

However, this paper relies too much on unproved intuitions. Consider the following paragraph from page 4:

> In natural language, whilst it is not the case that all sentences can be permuted without changing the meaning, it is the case that many sentences can be re-arranged, without much affecting a human’s understanding. For example, we feel that ‘box red’ is easily understandable, zero-shot, by a human. Thus we feel that a Receiver with similar compositional inductive bias to a human should be able to acquire quickly SHUF.
> 

While an interesting motivation, it is unfair to use the intuition that "box red" *should be* understandable to a human as a basis for saying what a machine should be able to do in a completely unnatural scenario that looks nothing like natural language. The primary reason I find this problematic is that we really have no immediate evidence that this kind of compositionality is amenable to humans, especially in arbitrary scenarios. Is "review open" the same as open review? I think there is room for much disagreement.

The second, more important, reason why this is not appropriate reasoning is that the authors focus on that kinds of things that they claim humans *shouldn't* be able to do, for which there is even less evidence, especially since it is harder to prove a negative. There is a basic flaw in the argument of this paper: surely we believe there are plenty of machines which can capture human-like compositionality in many cases, but can also capture inhuman composotionality just as well? Yet the authors depend on the idea that a machine that has inductive bias towards compositionality should not be able to learn compositional languages that the authors consider too artificial to be human-like, without providing quantitative evidence that these languages are so artificial they violate compositional inductive bias. The "No Free Lunch" theorem is even brought-up, as *not* being violated by divergence among learning rates for the different categories of grammars by different models. But if acquisition speeds between the different grammars presented aren't at least partially mutually exclusive, then why does the bench mark rely on relative acquisition speeds as a metric for measuring inductive bias?

In terms of reproducibility, the paper is somewhat messily reported, making reproducing it difficult. For instance, Tables 2 & 3 do not describe the units for the numbers they report. Code will help with this, but the main body of the text should be clear and accurate without reference to the code.

Details:

- Page #1—"Tabular rasa" → "Tabula rasa"
- There is no reason for a related work section (4) that merely points at the introduce, simply include the extra paragraph in the introduction.
- Tables 2 & 3 do not list units for any of the values.
content.summary_of_the_review: I feel that the motivation of measuring how quickly models fit a non-compositional grammar in order to measure compositional inductive bias is fundamentally flawed, at least in the very general way the authors claim it can be used. On top of this, the authors often rely on intuitive reasoning to justify what a given metric or experiment is measuring, intuition that sometimes seems valid, but is not solidified by evidence. To make a claim about this benchmark actually measuring compositionality, I feel that the authors would need to make that case that agents that do poorly on it are not likely to make compositional languages and that case is simply not made in this paper. Therefore, I recommend this paper to be rejected.

display_title: Official Review of Paper337 by Reviewer Qy6J

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a series of artificial grammars, including a non-compositional holistic one and a compositional one where object attributes map to message "words/sub-messages". Other grammars include various types of transformations of the compositional grammar that retain the compositional information in the message but do not abide by our intuitive visual notions of compositionality nor previously-proposed metrics in the literature to measure compositionality. The authors also propose a metric to measure compositionality, called the compositional entropy (CompEnt), which measures the reduction in the entropy of an object attribute on observing the message partition (based on token location) that has maximum mutual information with that attribute in the dataset. The authors evaluate models such as MLPs, RNNs, transformers, and a new architecture HU-RNN, on the proposed grammars using CompEnt and other metrics from the literature. They show which models have an inductive bias for which grammars by studying the speed of acquisition of the grammars for the different models. Specifically, the authors show that it is possible to construct languages with compositional information which perform poorly on existing compositionality metrics but are acquired quickly by popular neural models.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
- I like the chosen artificial grammars, they show that neural models don't necessarily have a preference for acquiring the compositional representation that is intuitive to humans or measurable by existing metrics.
- I appreciate the benchmarks verifying if the observed results are dependent on the number of parameters or not.

Weaknesses:
- There is some inconsistency between the models reported in Tables 2-5. Why are transformers from Table 2 not reported in Tables 3-5? HU-RNN can possibly be included in Tables 2-5 to make the same point as they do in Table 6 and the text can refer to those instead of a separate table.
- There are no indications of the variance of these results. What are the confidence intervals? The LSTM in Tables 2-5 seem to have different results than the one in Table 6, is this due to different sampling? If so, it shows that there can be a significant variance in these numbers.
- The paper has a few different goals, but it is not clear by the end of the Abstract and Introduction how they tie together in a coherent story.
- There is no statement that clearly describes what "Icy" is. I understand it as "a collection of grammars to evaluate compositional inductive bias of models". Is this correct?

Further questions and suggestions:
- Are the PROJ grammars always bijective? One can imagine based on some P that the same message can be reused for different objects. In such a case, perhaps it is expected that some models acquire this "partially collapsed" language faster than COMP.
- For SHUF, in the text "the permutation is sampled uniformly once per utterance in the language", does it mean you take a compositional language, and then shuffle the sub-messages of every possible message randomly? Why is this grammar proposed? It seems to just be adding noise to compositional grammars and is not reported in the results.
- For SHUFDET, my understanding is that the permutation for each possible message depends on the value of the first attribute. The example in Table 1 does not make this clear: is SHUFDET based on the last (right-most) attribute in this case?
- In Section 5.8, how well are the senders and receivers trained on their respective grammars? If they all acquired their grammar equally well, the accuracies in Figure 3 would start at the same point. For instance, it looks like PROJ has an advantage because the PROJ senders and receivers have acquired PROJ better than, say, the COMP senders and receivers acquiring COMP.
- Slightly more discussion in words of what equation 1 represents and why that's a meaningful metric to use would be helpful.
- What are HUSendZ:RNN, HUSendZ:dgsend? The paper describes what HUSendZ is, but not what these suffixes indicate.
- The Related work section is awkward. If it only has one paragraph of extra information, maybe it can find a place in Section 1 or 2 while removing the related work section altogether (since the references are already discussed in Introduction and Background).
- For visualizing the examples in Table 1, perhaps you can add in color? For example, color every "word" of COMP differently, and then maintain those colors for the rest of the examples so we can visually see how the message parts are being moved around for PERM, SHUF, SHUFDET. The other grammars can remain black to indicate that the mapping is not straightforward.
- In Section 2.1: In the text "is the number of objects in the object space O, e.g. Lazaridou et al. (2018)", it is more clear to write something like "same as Lazaridou et al. (2018)". In "When presented to a neural network, o is represented as the concatenation of $n_{att}$ $n_{val}$-hot vectors.", do you mean $n_{att}$ $n_{val}$-dimensional one-hot vectors instead?
- In Section 3.1: In the 3.1.x subsubsection headers, I would suggest putting the shorthands in parentheses instead of separating by commas.
- In Section 3.2: The text "section 7 tre" is a bit awkward -- TRE should be capitalized and perhaps the acronym TRE7 should be introduced beforehand and used here. Also, write "compositional entropy (CompEnt)" here as you are introducing this shorthand for the first time.
- In Section 3.5: Regarding HU-RNN, generally, the "upper" layer comes after the "lower" layer in deep learning convention, so the wording is a bit confusing because in this case, the lower layer seems to be after the upper layer.
- First sentence in Section 5.8 mentions "end-to-end" twice.
- In Section 6: "Icy" in the conclusion has different typesetting than the rest of the text.
- "In our own work" feels overused. I think you can cut "own" from this. You can also get away without having to justify something is "due to space constraints". You can present what you can and refer to the rest in the appendix, and the readers will know that it is to keep space.

Another interesting question to ask: Consider what happens when a subset of a grammar is used as training data. This would give an indication into what kind of grammars are actually likely to be acquired in the realistic scenario where the training data does not encompass the entire data space. It would be interesting to see which grammars have quick training data acquisition but retain poor generalization -- these are languages that the models have an inductive bias for that do not necessarily generalize.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper provides valuable insights for the future direction of language emergence research. It helps us understand which languages models have an inductive bias for and their relationship with compositionality and the existing metrics to measure compositionality. I would be in support of accepting this paper, but there are various concerns detailed in my review that I would like to see addressed for the paper to be ready for publication.

replying_to: Replying to Icy: A benchmark for measuring compositional inductive bias of emergent communication models
display_title: Official Review of Paper337 by Reviewer iPy9

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents a new benchmark called ICY, which measure compositional inductive bias of ML architectures. This is explored in the context of a signaling game, where the Sender should map an object (e.g., "red box") to a message (e.g., "adab"), and the Receiver should encoder this message back into an object.

The benchmark is obtained by transforming an original Sender/Receiver dataset in various ways. These transformations are meant to reduce the compositionality of the dataset, but the goal is that ML models can still fit to them easily. They also propose a new architecture called HU-RNN, which has an inductive bias that helps it do well on ICY. Finally, the propose a new metric for compositionality called Compositional Entropy.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
* Understanding the relation between what we humans perceive as "compositional", and whether this type of compositionality is difficult to learn for ML models is an important topic. 
* The ICY benchmark is potentially interesting since it contains a number of variations on a compositional language, allowing one to view compositional from different angles.

Weaknesses:
* Overall, In my opinion, the paper is currently too messy and the presentation is too confusing for acceptance. I provide a list of suggestions for improving the presentation below.
* The motivation of the paper is not clear to me. The paper state "we search for languages which models can fit to easily, but which a human might consider non-compositional" --> why is this interesting? Can you make this more specific? Just looking at this motivation, it actually seems very easy to me to find such languages. Consider for instance a language that maps A -> 0, B -> 1, C -> 2. Now we can create examples {[ABC, 012], [AAA, 000], ..., ]. It seems very easy to me for a model to learn this, but they are not perceived compositional to humans. I suspect you actually have a much better motivation in mind, but believe you aren't explaining it properly.

Overal suggestions for improving the presentation:
* Better separate out related work. Currently there is quite some related work in Section 1, Section 2, and Section 4 (which is actually called "Related work", but contains almost no related work).
* Reduce the number of sections. Currently it almost seems every paragraph has its own subsection, which doesn't read well.
* Better motivate the ICY dataset. Why exactly are these transformations important?
* Better introduce the dataset. Right now I miss some basic introduction to the dataset. What does it contain exactly? How big is it? How did you build it?
* Add more details to the new architecture you are introducing: HU-RNN. That seems to be one of the innovations, but it isn't explained well. In fact, it almost has as much explanation as an RNN (which I think everybody knows, so you can just leave out the formulas there).

There are plenty of mistakes / typos / unclarities, of which I list a few below:

* Section 1
  - metrics such as posdis and bosdis are sometimes capitalized and sometimes not
  - and measuring --> and measure
  - only considers --> only consider

* Section 2
  - Are n_{att} and n_{val} disjoint? They are drawn from the same vocabulary so it may be worth clarifying that.
  - It looks like all attributes have the same about of possible values, since the vocab size is n_{att} x n_{val}. Is this true? It is a somewhat odd assumption.
  - co-ordinate --> coordinate
  - When trained using REINFORCE you obtain a language with |G| messages. It seems this language is holistic since it has one message for each (attribute,value) pair, is that correct? It may be worth clarifying.
  - composition function --> composition functions
  - to be concatenation --> to be the concatenation
  - explicitly incorporates --> explicitly incorporate

* Section 3
  - What is the o_n^{(j)} notation? How does it relate to Section 2.1 explaining the general framework?
  - sub-message w_{j, o_n^{(j)}} --> shouldn't the first "j" be an "i"?
  - Generally Section 3.1.1 is quite confusing
  - in Sect 3.1.4 you hypothesize outputs from an NN can be arbitrarily rotated. Do you mean projected? This is namely what you need to do in this subsection.
  - time-step, project it --> time step and project it
  - In the def of an RNN there is a right parenthesis missing.
  - In Section 3.2 you say "Since we have c_{len} > n_{att}", how does this follow?
  - "We wanted to use in addition residual entropy" --> consider rephrasing
  - In Section 3.3 you say you will introduce the models in the experimental section, but you actually seem to do it directly afterwards.
 
* Section 5
  - Figure 2 actually seems to show that TRE gives lower scores to COMP and PERM, but that seems to disagree with what is said in the text. Perhaps TRE assigns lower scores when the compositionality is higher? If so, please clarify this.
  - Table 2: it would be useful to explain what the numbers mean in the caption as well.
  - This section does experiments on the ICY benchmark, but the benchmark itself is never introduced, while it seems to be the main contribution of this paper.
  - In Section 5.3 you conclude "Thus, current neural models will tend to produce output that is not considered compositional to humans". I find this conclusion very odd and I don't agree with it.

* Section 6
  - communicaiton --> communication

display_title: New section 'human evaluation'

content.title: New section 'human evaluation'
content.comment:
We thank you very much for the reviews. They are very insightful and informative, and we appreciate very much the thought, time, effort, and expertise that has gone into them.

We note that a major consensus across all reviews was the lack of human evaluation. This manifested itself as comments such as:
- missing human trials to substantiate some of the claims
- too many unproved intuitions

Therefore, we have spent our rebuttal period on setting up an MTurk task, running this, and evaluating the results. We have moved some sections into the appendix, to make space, and added a new 'human evaluations' section. We have rewritten the title, the abstract, the claims, and the conclusion, to take into account both the presence of human evaluation experiments, and their results.

We did feel originally, when writing the original paper, that it would be good to have human evaluation, but we were hoping that this would be something that could go into a future paper. However, given the broad consensus that without them, there are far too many unproved intuitions, and unsubstantiated claims, we have added human evaluation. We do like the paper much more now, it does feel more complete/balanced to us. We hope that this may address some of the concerns that were raised in the original reviews.

The new 'human evaluation' section is described briefly in the body, at the start of the 'Experiments' section, and more completely at the end of the appendix.

To avoid having to open the revised paper to see the changes, here is the contents of the mturk write-up from the paper body (minus the screenshot):

***

## Human evaluation

[Screenshot of 'Secret Spy Codes' game here]

We constructed an MTurk \citep{mturk} task, `Secret Spy Codes', in order to evaluate human performance on \textsc{Icy} grammars. Figure \ref{fig:mturk_full} shows the user interface. Human subjects were tasked with writing out the code that represents depicted geometric objects.
They needed substantial effort in order to learn just a few new words.
Thus, we used objects with only two attributes: shape and color; and we experimented with using abbreviated English words, which were easier to learn.

### Dataset

\textsc{synth} uses artificially generated random words for each attribute value. We sample 2-letter words from a vocabulary size of 4. Each utterance therefore has 4 letters: 2 for shape, and 2 for color. Since humans found these words challenging to learn, so we used just three possible values for each attribute, giving 9 combinations in total.

\textsc{eng} uses 3-letter English abbreviations for attribute values, e.g. 'tri' for 'triangle', and 'grn' for 'green'. The words describing each attribute value in \textsc{eng} are relatively easy for a human to learn. Therefore, we used 5 attribute values for each attribute, giving 25 possible combinations.

We held out three color-shape combinations, that were not made available during training. For example, subjects might have access to a red circle and a blue triangle, but not a red triangle. Subjects who could perceive the compositional structure of a grammar should be able to get these holdout instances correct.

### Evaluation

[Results table here]

We measured subjects performance in two ways: across all test examples, and uniquely on the 3 held out examples. The results are shown in Table \ref{tab:turk_results}. We can see that in the \textsc{synth} scenario, $\acc_{holdout}$ was poor for all grammars: humans were unable to spot any type of compositional form in unfamiliar words. In the \textsc{eng} scenario, $\acc_{holdout}$ was high for both \textsc{comp} and \textsc{shufdet} grammars, as expected, and low for all other grammars. This shows that the composition functions in \textsc{perm}, \textsc{proj} and \textsc{rot} were not clearly apparent to human subjects, even though, as we shall see next, neural models can acquire these grammars easily.

content.comment: Thank you for conducting human evaluation, as I think this is definitely a necessary component that was left out of the original paper. replying_to: Replying to clarification
display_title: Reponse

content.title: Reponse
content.comment:
There are two parts to any utterance:
- the words, which map to each individual attribute. For example, 'blu' as a color, and 'tri' as a shape
- the composition function, which combines the words for each meaning together, to form an utterance

For our own purposes, what we care about in this paper is the composition function, the second part. The various composition functions we present in our work can be applied for a broad family of words. We assume that each word has the same number of letters, with no intervening spaces. Thus we abbreviate the english words to be each 3 letters, and remove spaces.

The shape words we use are:

- cir (='circle')
- tri (='triangle')
- box ('box')
- pnt (='pentagon')
- hex (='hexagon')

And the color words are:

- blu (='blue')
- red
- grn (='green')
- yel (='yellow')
- mag (='magenta')

Then, using a concatenation grammar, an uttearnce could look like 'pntyel'. Using a permutation grammar, an utterance could look like 'tpynle'.

By using abbreviations of English words, we avoid the workers needing to memorize new words for each attribute, and they can focus their attention on trying to detect any composition function between them. (We do not instruct them to search for composition, we simply present them with colored shapes, and instruct them to learn to describe them with secret codes).

Similarly, here is the new title, abstract, and claims:

### Title: Neural networks can understand compositional functions that humans do not, in the context of emergent communication

### Abstract

"We show that it is possible to craft transformations that, applied to compositional grammars, result in grammars that neural networks can learn easily, but humans do not. This could explain the disconnect between current metrics of compositionality, that are arguably human-centric, and the ability of neural networks to generalize to unseen examples. We propose to use the transformations as a benchmark, \textsc{Icy}, which could be used to measure aspects of the compositional inductive bias of networks, and to search for networks with similar compositional inductive biases to humans. As an example of this approach, we propose a hierarchical model, HU-RNN, which shows an inductive bias towards position-independent, word-like groups of tokens. In addition, we find that Residual Entropy is slow to calculate for our geometries, so we propose a relaxation, `Compositional Entropy', that is fast, and broadly applicable."

***

Here is a more complete list of changes we made:
- moved end-to-end analysis to appendix
- moved shuf grammar to appendix
- moved 'Acquisition accuracy given fixed training budget' into appendix
- rewrote title, abstract, conclusion
- various localized changes, eg added parentheses around (section 7)
- removed 'related work' section
- added paragraph to ethics to say that we do not believe the models are `alive' or 'conscious', but admitting that we have no way to objectively prove this
- added paragraph to ethics for the mturk experiments
- added color to example utterances in table 1

***

Updated claims:

- demonstrate transformations, which we can apply to compositional grammars which give rise to grammars whose compositional structure:
    - appears to current metrics of compositionality as non-compositional
    - is opaque to humans
    - does not affect acquisition speed of neural models
- this could explain the empirical disconnect observed between metrics of compositionality, and generalization ability, in emergent communication languages
- we measure the performance of these transformations:
    - using current compositional metrics
    - using human evaluation
    - using a selection of standard neural models
- in addition we propose a transformation, which we show that humans can readily understand, but which neural models acquire slowly, which relocates word-like units within an utterance
- as an example of using our transformations to search for models with a compositional inductive bias more aligned with that of humans, we propose a model, HU-RNN, that shows faster acquisition speed for transforms that relocate word-like units within an utterance
- as part of our analysis, we wanted to use Residual Entropy, but found that its runtime is combinatorial, and prohibitively slow on our geometries. Therefore we propose a relaxed compositionality metric `Compositional Entropy', which is generally applicable, and fast to calculate

display_title: Some initial answers to questions and concerns raised in the reviews, 1

content.title: Some initial answers to questions and concerns raised in the reviews, 1
content.comment:
We have spent most of our time working on the new 'human evaluation' section, however, we have started to address some of the other points and questions raised. Here are some initial answers to some of the questions and concerns raised:

### if one message for each {attribute,value} pair then the language is holistic

For example (shape,square) could be 'box' and (color,red) could be 'red'. Combining the words for each (attribute,value) pair gives the utterance `redbox'. This is a compositional grammar, even though the word for each (attribute,value) pair is unique.

### are the PROJ grammars always bijective? perhaps models acquire the 'partially collapsed' language faster than COMP?

You are right. Whilst we do have a method to verify that grammars are bijective, we are only applying it to shuf and shufdet grammars. We should apply it to all grammars, and in particular to proj, since, as you point out, it does seem very possible that the transformation is not in fact bijective, and does reduce the expressivity of the resulting language. We would be happy to add in at least a measure of empirically to what extent the resulting grammars do deviate from bijective grammars. We admit we did not have time to do that yet, during this ~two week rebuttal period, but it seems like something we could add in in time for the camera-ready version.

### what happens when a subset of a grammar is used as training data. which grammars have quick training data generalization but retain poor generalization. these are languages that the models have an inductive bias for but that do not necessarily generalize

We agree that this would be an interesting set of experiments to run, especially given that the new human evaluations are testing for generalization, rather than acquisition speed.

### paper somewhat messily reported, eg tables 2&3 do not describe the units for the numbers they report

The results are the ratio of the convergence times for the grammar, relative to comp grammar. Therefore there are no units. We have added a clarification on this point into the heading for table 2.

### missing human trials to substantiate some of the claims
### too many unproved intuitions
### need to make the case that agents that do poorly on the benchmark are not likely to make compositional languages

We have added in a new 'human evaluation' section, where we measure human performance on these grammars. Our results show that indeed humans are not able to perceive the compositional structure in our transformed grammars. Except for shufdet, which humans were able to understand almost as well as comp (and much more easily than perm).

### 'perm' should actually be considered compositional

Technically yes, because the strict definition of compositionality requires only that the utterance representing two sub-utterances is the composition of the two sub-utterances, where the composition function can be arbitrary. For example the projection of the concatenation of the two sub-utterances is a valid composition function, though not one amenable to human understanding. This is one of the key points we intend to make: neural models can perceive compositional functions that humans do not.

Empirically, our human evaluation section shows that humans are in fact unable to perceive a constant permutation function of the concatenation of two sub-utterances as being compositional.

### what particular properties of compositionality are the metrics measuring?

Well, right: as a community, our metrics of compositionality are human-centric, correspond to composition functions that humans use, typically concatenation. None of the existing metrics take into account the possibility of e.g. adding a projection function into the composition function. And if we want emergent communication scenarios to emerge languages that humans can perceive as compositional, then we want our metrics to align with human-perceivable composition functions. Nevertheless, just because humans can only perceive certain subsets from the space of all possible composition functions does not mean that the remaining space of composition functions are invalid composition functions. Indeed, as we show, we can find composition functions in the remaining space which neural models can understand/acquire quickly, but which humans cannot.

Our benchmark therefore shows some of the specific composition functions that neural models can understand, but which humans cannot.

display_title: Some initial answers to questions and concerns raised in the reviews, 2

content.title: Some initial answers to questions and concerns raised in the reviews, 2
content.comment:
### explain 'thus, current neural models will tend to produce output that is not considered compositional to humans'

Since neural models can perceive composition functions that humans do not, as shown by the combination of our human evaluation studies, and our neural evaluation studies, so two neural models, in an emergent communication scenario, can agree on a composition function that generates language that is not considered compositional by humans. This not to say that the composition function used by the neural models is not a valid composition function, just that humans would not recognize it as such.

### for SHUFDET, example in table 1 does not make cler: is SHUFDET based  on the last (right-most) attribute in this case?

Yes, you are right. Corrected this in the shufdet description.

### concatenation of n_att n_val-hot vectors. do you mean n_val-dimensional one-hot vectors?

Right :)

### perhaps add color to visualizations in table 1?

Good idea. Thanks! We have added this :)

### Consider for instance a language that maps A -> 0, B -> 1, C -> 2. Now we can create examples {[ABC, 012], [AAA, 000], ..., ]. It seems very easy to me for a model to learn this, but they are not perceived compositional to humans

We are not sure we understand. It looks like you are simply mapping from one token representation to another? Wouldn't this be orthogonal to any specific grammar? We understand a human might not be able to easily read the resulting cipher, but we feel that a cipher won't change the actual underlying compositional structure?

In defense of your claim though, we note that in the human evaluation section, when using the 'synth' dataset, humans did in fact struggle to recognize compositional structure, so this does support your hypothesis that a simple cipher is sufficient to prevent humans from recognizing compositional structure.

### Are n_{att} and n_{val} disjoint? They are drawn from the same vocabulary so it may be worth clarifying that.

n_att and n_val are orthogonal. They describe the dimensions of the meaning space. They are not drawn from a vocabulary, but define the dimensions of the meaning space vocabulary. i.e. there is a different token for each possible value of {1, ..., n_att} and {1, ..., n_val}. In practice, in our codebase implementation, we share the token vocabulary across all attributes, e.g. a specific meaning could be babc, where each letter represents a single attribute, and the vocabulary is {a,b,c, ...}. However, we use the notation from Resnick et al 2020, section 3.1, because we felt this made some details of exposition clearer.

### It looks like all attributes have the same amout of possible values, since the vocab size is n_{att} x n_{val}. Is this true? It is a somewhat odd assumption.

Do you mean, because in reality there might be 5 possible shapes, and 10 possible colors, for example? This is true in the general case, however for simplicity we kept the number of possible values of each attribute identical. You can see that we did this also in the human evaluation: 'eng' dataset has 5 colors and 5 shapes, whereas 'synth' has 3 colors and 3 shapes. i.e. 'eng' has n_att = 2 and n_val = 5; whereas 'synth' has n_att=2 and n_val = 3.

### When trained using REINFORCE you obtain a language with |G| messages. It seems this language is holistic since it has one message for each (attribute,value) pair, is that correct? It may be worth clarifying.

A compositional language with perfect expressivity will also have a unique message for each possible meaning. The difference between a compositional language and a holistic language is that a compositional utterance can be formed from a composition function taking in sub-utterances. Thus, given a sub-utterance describing a shape, and another describing a color, in a compositional language we can apply a composition function g(., .) to the sub-utterances to obtain an utterance describing both the shape and the color. In a holistic language, there is no way to predict the utterance for a specific shape and color given a sub-utterance for the shape, and one for the color. compositional: 'red' + 'box' => 'redbox'. Non-compositional might look like 'red' + 'box' => 'fnvjghe' (though one cannot tell from the resulting utterance whether it is actually compositional, eg it might have been formed from the projection of the concatenation, as we describe in our paper).

display_title: Some initial answers to questions and concerns raised in the reviews, 3

content.title: Some initial answers to questions and concerns raised in the reviews, 3
content.comment:
### In Section 3.2 you say "Since we have c_{len} > n_{att}", how does this follow?

We are using allocating space in the message for 4 tokens per meaning attribute. This means that c_{len} = 4 * n_{att}, and therefore c_{len} > n_{att}. It is an arbitrary geometry choice. Some papers, eg the posdis/bosdis paper, "Compositionality and Generalization in Emergent Languages", Chaabouni et al, allocate space for a single message token per meaning attribute. However, we feel that this is different from human natural language, in which we have several message tokens (i.e. a word) to describe each meaning (e.g. the word `red' describes one single color). Therefore we are using a geometry that allows for word-like representations for each attribute.

### In Section 5.3 you conclude "Thus, current neural models will tend to produce output that is not considered compositional to humans". I find this conclusion very odd and I don't agree with it.

What makes you feel that neural models do produce output this is considered compositional to humans? There are papers, e.g. Lazaridou et al  2018, that show that some compositional structure can emerge. However, other papers, e.g. Andreas "Measuring compositionality" show that if one samples many languages, from multiple experimental runs, some will show measurable compositionality, and some will not, and those that do not show measurable compositionality often still are able to generalize well to unseen meanings. We show that it is possible that the output considered as 'non-compositional' from emergent communication games may in fact be compositional, but just not using compositional functions that are readily apparent either to human observation, or to our human-centric metrics of compositionality. Is the projection of the concatenation of sub-utterances compositional? Well, yes, technically it is. Can humans recognize such utterances as being the composition of the sub-utterances? Our human evaluation shows that they do not.

display_title: New version: rewrote introduction, removed compositional entropy, renamed comp grammar to concat

content.title: New version: rewrote introduction, removed compositional entropy, renamed comp grammar to concat
content.comment:
We have just now submitted a new revision. The major changes are:
- rewritten introduction
- clarified our definition of compositionality, and defined three subsets of compositional space: 'generalizable compositionality', 'human compositionality', and 'neural compositionality'
- renamed 'compositional' grammar to 'concatenation' grammar (and abbreviation 'comp' renamed to 'concat')
- moved compositional entropy metric into appendix, renamed to HCE ('human compositional entropy'), and removed from claims (in order to free up space)

To save opening the pdf, here is the new introduction text (excluding the claims section):

***

Statistical association language models produce impressive results in domains such as summarization, and few-shot learning (e.g. \citet{zhang2020pegasus}, or \citet{brown2020language}).
However, it is unclear to what extent such tasks require creative invention by the neural models.
Thus, we target a slightly different task of `emergent communication'.
Tabula rasa agents placed in a collaborative scenario emerge their own communicative code (e.g. \citet{lazaridou2018_refgames} and \citet{foerster_multi_agent_rl_2016}).
We wish to reproduce aspects of the development of human natural language (e.g. \citet{pinker1990natural}, \citet{berwick2012bird}).
A key aspect is compositionality: the meaning of an utterance is a function of the meaning of the parts.
Agents in emergent communication scenarios empirically do not naturally produce compositional output, as measured by human evaluation, and by compositional metrics, e.g. \citet{kottur2017natural}.

\citet{kirby2008cumulative} showed in human experiments that artificial languages evolved to become more compositional when transmitted from one human to another.
However, in the case of artificial models, \citet{griffiths2007language} showed that for a broad range of conditions, transmission of languages across generations converges to the prior.
For artificial models, a key question thus is: what are the priors? To what extent do commonly used models incorporate a compositional inductive bias?

[Venn diagram of compositionality space]

To go further, we need a concrete definition of compositionality. We use the definition of compositionality from \citet{andreas_measuring_compositionality_2019}:
an utterance representing the combined meaning of two sub-utterances should be a deterministic function $g(\cdot, \cdot)$ of the two sub-utterances. 
This is a broad definition of compositionality, and includes holistic mappings, which do not generalize.
We thus consider two subsets of compositionlity, which we term 'generalizable' compositionility, and 'human' compositionality. Human compositionality is defined to be compositional functions which can be used by humans. Generalizable composition is defined to be any composition function which allows generalization.
Figure \ref{fig:composition_venn} depicts these subsets of composition space, as well as a subset `neural', depicting composition functions usable by current neural models.

Our current metrics of composition implicitly target human compositionality. We hypothesize that a consistently observed disconnect between the measured compositionality of emergent communication grammars, and their ability to generalize \citep{chaabouni2020compositionality}, is a direct consequence of our metrics of compositionality targeting human compositionality.

We present specific examples of generalizable composition functions, which neural models can acquire easily, but which humans do not recognize as compositional, and which current compositional metrics consider to be non-compositional. In addition, we present a grammar, \textsc{shufdet}, whose composition humans can understand but which neural models cannot. We propose a novel neural architecture, HU-RNN, that can acquire \textsc{shufdet} faster than other neural models.

What we can learn from this is three-fold. Firstly, when we talk about compositionality, we should be clear about whether we mean human compositionality, generalizable compositionality, or some other kind of compositionality. Secondly, we should be clear about what our goal is when we wish for emergent communication games to emerge compositional language. Is our goal to make the language should appear to be compositional to humans, or simply that the language appear compositional to neural networks?
Thirdly the compositional inductive bias of current neural networks is quite different from that of humans: there are generalizable compositions that neural networks can use that humans cannot; and 
similarly there are compositional functions, e.g \textsc{shufdet}, that humans can use that current neural networks do not.

replying_to: Replying to New version: rewrote introduction, removed compositional entropy, renamed comp grammar to concat
display_title: definitions of compositionality

content.title: definitions of compositionality
content.comment:
I really like the idea of splitting up compositionality notions into those which humans use in language, and those which are technically compositional but don't align with human intuitions of what compositionality should look like (or at least they are not learnable by humans). However, this doesn't explicitly characterize human compositionality from a rigorous standpoint. I recognize this maybe out of the scope of your particular paper, but I would treat it as somewhat essential at least to mention. As is, the particular metrics you've chosen seem to target something more about researcher psychology (what makes us select these particular functions as compositional?) rather than compositionality broadly. What sort of rules do you consider to be human composition, rather than generalizable composition? I see you've classified projection as a compositional function, but are there any compositional rules that wouldn't be easily learned by a human but would be readable by a human if described adequately? In particular, I'm asking about whether there are classes of compositional grammars that are not intuitive to humans but are not completely unreadable (due to being a raw vector).

Without a more in depth characterization of the distinction between human and general compositionality, the line of argument in this paper doesn't have the rigor that I would want from it. You can either measure a model as more compositional, or as more human-like in its compositional capabilities. These are two different properties you are measuring, and you still haven't positioned yourself to argue the second, which is where you're transitioning to in the revisions. This positioning would require more understanding of human and nonhuman compositional behavior.

I definitely think more rigor about these distinctions is essential, and would clarify your line of thought. Your changes have
improved the paper. Unfortunately, I still don't think it's complete as is.

Also, you might want to briefly proofread for typos (compositionlity)

replying_to: Replying to definitions of compositionality
display_title: We define human compositionality as that which a human can use

content.title: We define human compositionality as that which a human can use
content.comment:
We define human compositionality as that which a human can use. This is the gold standard definition we create. Thus, there is no theoretical way to decide whether a composition function is humanly compositional or not: it is an empirical question. We provide some small first experiments in the direction of measuring some composition functions that humans are not able to use. But of course, it is entirely possible that someone else could present the exact same composition functions to humans in a slightly different way, and obtain different results. We do not pretend to know what a human can or cannot do, any more than we can claim what a neural network can or cannot do.

We feel that at least explicitly calling out the different types and goals of compositionality is a perhaps a good start to clarifying much of the existing work on compositionality, which we feel implicitly assumes 'human' compositionality, but without explictly stating so.

c4bC,

We didn't have time to post yet, since concentrating on updating the revisions, prior to deadline tonight, but we would like to thank you tremendously for your observation that we were abusing the word 'compositionality', not defining it, and using it to mean different things at different times. These observations were we felt extremely insightful, and spot on, and were what inspired us to think more clearly about what do we mean by compositional, how to define it, and ultimately to allow holistic functions to be compositional, which they are, per a strict definition of compositionality, and to define smaller subsets of composition function, with clearly defined names and definitions.

display_title: Thanks for the compliment!

content.title: Thanks for the compliment!
content.comment:
I'm really glad that your paper has improved so much by clarifying your meaning about compositionality! Compositionality is a multifaceted concept that can reflect as much about researcher psychology as about a specific technical property. I think a good discussion of these facets is in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.08351.pdf

To clarify my meaning about making the distinction more rigorous, I agree that you can't theoretically describe how a human is able to perform compositional functions. However, you can describe this empirically, and there is a body of cognitive science literature about what human biases exist in learning artificial languages. I would look into some of the work of Simon Kirby's lab as an example: https://pure.mpg.de/rest/items/item_3190925_14/component/file_3219601/content#page=71 (but look through recent work in general from that group, there's a lot of work around exploring how language develops in communication games between humans)

Overall, I think that this work is promising now that you have started to clarify more of your thinking around what compositionality means and what types of compositionality you are interested in measuring and contrasting. While I don't believe that the turnaround time for this rebuttal has been enough for you to make the paper ready for publication, I encourage you to continue pursuing this project. If you clarify your own thinking around this enough, this work can help a lot of other researchers in this space clarify their thinking as well.

content.title: new version fleshes out description of HCE metric, in the appendix
content.comment:
new version fleshes out description of HCE metric, in the appendix.

Added to start of exposition of HCE:

***

We relax the minimization in the Residual Entropy metric \citep{resnick2019}. Resnick defines residual entropy as:

[Formula here]

where $\mathcal{M}$ is the space of messages, $i$ is an index over attributes, $o^{(i)}$ is the i'th attribute, $\mathcal{P}$ is the set of all possible partitions over the messages, $p$ is one such partition, $p_i$ is one set in the partition $p$, $z[p_i]$ is the sub-sequence of each message indexed by set $p_i$, and $\mathcal{H}$ is the entropy. Thus, residual entropy finds a partition over messages, into $n_{att}$ sets, which associates each set in the partition with a specific attribute $\in \{1, \dots, n_{att}\}$, and minimizes the conditional entropy between each attribute in the dataset, and the corresponding message sub-sequences.

We can see that residual entropy assumes a composition that comprises a permutation over concatenation. This is thus a measure of human compositionality. It does not attempt to measure other members of the class of generalizable composition functions.

The minimization over $p \in \mathcal{P}$ is problematic because it involves a minimization over a combinatorial number of partitions. We seek to relax this, by using a greedy approach, to avoid the combinatorial minimization.

***

And modified last paragraph of HCE exposition to:

***
HCE has similar speed advantages to posdis and bosdis, but assumes only $c_{len} \ge n_{att}$. posdis and bosdis provide alternative relaxations of residual entropy, but they both require that $c_{len} = n_{att}$.
HCE lies in $[0, 1]$, in alignment with topsim, bosdis, and posdis.
We present empirical comparisons between resent and HCE next.

content.comment:
Latest revision adds section 2.3 'other work on compositionality', which adds back in paragraph of references cut during introduction rewrite, and adds in references to White et al, and Hupke et al

***

"One approach to investigating the compositional inductive biases of models is to run many emergent communication experiments. This is time-consuming, noisy, and entangles many factors of variation.
Importantly, it is unclear how to inspect the compositional characteristics of the resulting languages.
We choose an alternative approach of generating languages which exhibit specific deviations from a perfectly compositional language; and measuring how easily each model can fit these artificial languages.
Our approach is similar to that used in \citet{libowling_easeofteaching}, \citet{kharitonov-baroni-2020-acquisition} and \citet{resnick2019}. However, \citet{libowling_easeofteaching} only considers a single transformation (permutation); \citet{kharitonov-baroni-2020-acquisition} focus on the effect of compositionality on generalization; and \citet{resnick2019} investigates primarily the effect of capacity.
\citet{hupke_compositionality_decomposed_2020} and \citet{white_inductive_bias_neural_lm_artificial_lang} use artificially created languages to test neural model's understanding of compositional forms that appear in natural language.
In our work, we search for languages which models can fit to easily, but which a human might consider non-compositional."
